symptoms: Olive-green to dull velvety black spots on leaves and fruit
Leaves become curled, distorted, and drop prematurely
Superficial corky brown scabs developing on fruit surface
actions: Apply protective fungicide (captan or copper-based) during green-tip through petal-fall stages
Rake and safely compost or destroy fallen overwintering leaves
Prune tree canopy to improve sunlight penetration and accelerate leaf drying
preventative: Plant scab-resistant cultivars such as Liberty, Prima, or Enterprise
Space trees adequately to maximize aeration across rows

symptoms: Frog-eye leaf spots with purple margins and tan necrotic centers
Firm, brown fruit rot expanding with concentric dark rings
Sunken cankers on bark and branch dieback
actions: Prune out dead wood, fire blight strikes, and mummified fruit
Apply thiophanate-methyl or captan fungicide according to regional advisory
Disinfect pruning shears between cuts with 70% isopropyl alcohol
preventative: Maintain tree vigor with balanced nutrition and avoid drought stress
Inspect bark annually for winter freeze injury and canker formation

symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish spots on upper leaf surfaces
Raised tube-like fungal aecia forming on the underside of leaves
Early seasonal defoliation during moist spring weather
actions: Apply myclobutanil or propiconazole fungicide between pink bud and petal fall
Remove nearby Eastern red cedar and juniper galls within a 1-mile radius where feasible
Maintain regular scouting following rainfall events above 10°C
preventative: Select rust-immune apple cultivars (e.g., Freedom, Redfree, Liberty)
Avoid planting apple orchards adjacent to ornamental juniper windbreaks

symptoms: Uniform rich green leaf pigmentation across upper canopy
Smooth leaf margins free of lesions, chlorosis, or necrotic spots
Vigorous shoot growth and healthy terminal buds
actions: Maintain scheduled seasonal irrigation based on soil moisture tensiometers
Conduct routine leaf petiole tissue testing for nutrient balance
preventative: Maintain orchard sanitation and integrated pest monitoring traps

symptoms: Glossy, dark green leaves without chlorotic mottling or edge scorch
Uniform branch elongation with vigorous fruit bud clusters
Healthy fibrous root system free of fungal root rot
actions: Maintain acidic soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2 using elemental sulfur
Ensure uniform moisture with drip irrigation under pine bark mulch
preventative: Annual soil testing to verify organic matter and micronutrient availability

symptoms: White talcum-like powdery fungal patches on young leaves and fruit
Upward leaf curling, distortion, and stunted terminal shoot growth
Web-like fungal mycelium expanding rapidly in warm, dry weather
actions: Apply sulfur, quinoxyfen, or myclobutanil fungicide at shuck fall
Prune dense inner water sprouts to promote canopy airflow
Avoid excessive spring nitrogen fertilization that drives succulent shoots
preventative: Plant resistant cherry cultivars in well-ventilated orchard sites
Monitor orchard microclimate for relative humidity peaks above 70%

symptoms: Lush emerald-green leaves with crisp serrated margins
No signs of shot-hole perforation, mildew, or viral leaf mottle
Normal fruit cluster development along spur branches
actions: Continue drip irrigation and seasonal canopy monitoring
Inspect weekly for spotted wing drosophila and aphids
preventative: Follow dormant copper and oil sprays prior to bud break

symptoms: Rectangular tan or gray lesions restricted by leaf veins
Lesions coalesce to blight large sections of the ear leaf and canopy
Premature plant senescence and lodging under heavy disease pressure
actions: Apply strobilurin or triazole fungicides before VT/R1 silking stage if thresholds are met
Chop and incorporate crop residue post-harvest to speed fungal breakdown
Prioritize field harvesting if stalk integrity is compromised
preventative: Plant maize hybrids with proven resistance to Gray Leaf Spot
Rotate fields with non-host crops such as soybean or alfalfa

symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture epidermal tissue releasing powdery brick-red urediniospores
Chlorotic bands surrounding dense pustule clusters
actions: Scout lower and middle leaves; apply foliar fungicide if pustules appear before silking
Avoid overhead irrigation during late afternoon hours
Ensure balanced soil potassium to bolster stalk cellular strength
preventative: Sow corn hybrids containing Rp gene resistance
Plant early in the season to evade southward spore-bearing wind currents

symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green or tan lesions
Lesions may extend 2.5 to 15 cm along the leaf blade
Extensive leaf desiccation leading to significant grain fill reduction
actions: Apply foliar fungicide (e.g., azoxystrobin + propiconazole) if lesions threaten the ear leaf
Deep-till infected residues post-harvest to reduce overwintering conidia
Monitor humidity and temperature conditions (18–27°C with extended dew)
preventative: Select hybrids carrying Ht resistance genes
Practice a minimum 2-year crop rotation out of continuous maize

symptoms: Robust, broad dark green leaf blades with sturdy central midrib
Turgid upright foliage without curling, wilting, or fungal lesions
Normal whorl expansion and vigorous tassel/ear development
actions: Support rapid vegetative stage (V6–V12) with planned side-dress nitrogen
Monitor soil moisture sensors to maintain optimal root zone saturation
preventative: Maintain weed-free cultivation rows and monitor for stem borers

symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with tiny black pycnidia specks
Berries shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies hanging on clusters
Dark elongated cankers along green shoots and tendrils
actions: Apply mancozeb, captan, or tebuconazole starting from early shoot growth to 4 weeks post-bloom
Prune and destroy all mummified grape clusters and infected canes during dormancy
Open vine canopy through canopy shoot positioning to dry cluster microclimate
preventative: Avoid low-lying vineyard blocks with poor cold-air drainage
Keep vineyard floor cleanly mowed or mulched

symptoms: Tiger-stripe interveinal leaf chlorosis and necrosis with green margins
Small dark purple or brown spots ('measles') on ripening berries
Internal wood apoplexy and sudden summer vine collapse
actions: Mark symptomatic vines for late-dormant remedial pruning or trunk renewal
Apply wound protectant paints containing flusilazole or Trichoderma to large cuts
Remove and burn dead vine trunks and cordon arms
preventative: Avoid making large pruning wounds during wet weather
Use certified clean pathogen-free grapevine nursery stock

symptoms: Irregular, angular reddish-brown lesions bounded by leaf veinlets
Dark velvety sporulation on the underside of necrotic leaf patches
Premature defoliation resulting in sunburned fruit and reduced sugar brix
actions: Apply copper-based or dithiocarbamate protective sprays during humid periods
Strip lower basal leaves around clusters to enhance air circulation
Manage vine vigor by moderating late-season irrigation and nitrogen
preventative: Prune canopy according to balanced trellis specifications
Scout vineyard rows weekly during late summer fruit ripening

symptoms: Expansive, deep green palmate leaves with vigorous shoot tips
Clean fruit clusters free of botrytis, mildew, or black rot lesions
Uniform leaf transpiration and balanced vine vigor
actions: Maintain regulated deficit irrigation (RDI) for optimal wine/table grape quality
Monitor microclimate temperature and humidity data
preventative: Routine canopy shoot tucking and IPM scouting for leafhoppers

symptoms: Asymmetrical blotchy mottle leaf yellowing across veins
Yellow shoots on individual canopy limbs (the 'yellow dragon')
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit with inverted coloration and aborted seeds
actions: Strictly control the Asian Citrus Psyllid (Diaphorina citri) vector using systemic insecticides and biological predators
Eradicate and remove confirmed infected trees to protect surrounding grove
Provide enhanced micronutrient foliar sprays (Zn, Mn, Fe, B) to sustain infected trees temporarily
preventative: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock from screenhouses
Establish regional citrus health management areas (CHMAs)

symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked purple or brown spots on leaves
Infected leaf centers drop out leaving a distinct 'shot-hole' appearance
Deep pitted, gumming lesions on developing peach fruit
actions: Apply protective bactericides (copper hydroxide or oxytetracycline) during spring bloom and petal fall
Avoid overhead irrigation that splashes bacterial cells between branches
Prune dead twig cankers during dry winter periods
preventative: Plant cultivars with genetic resistance (e.g., Clayton, Harrow Diamond)
Avoid high-wind orchard exposures by installing perimeter windbreaks

symptoms: Glossy lanceolate leaves with vibrant emerald green coloring
No shot-hole perforations, gumming, or leaf curl symptoms
Vigorous current-season shoot growth
actions: Continue drip irrigation and mulch maintenance around tree drip lines
Monitor for oriental fruit moth and peach tree borer
preventative: Standard dormant spray program with copper and superior horticultural oil

symptoms: Small, water-soaked dark green spots turning greasy brown with yellow halos
Severe premature defoliation exposing bell peppers to sunscald
Rough, raised, blister-like corky lesions on fruit
actions: Apply copper bactericide combined with mancozeb for enhanced bacterial knockdown
Avoid working in field rows when foliage is wet from morning dew or rain
Immediately remove and dispose of heavily infected individual plants
preventative: Use certified pathogen-free, hot-water-treated pepper seeds
Practice a 2 to 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants (tomato/eggplant/pepper)

symptoms: Smooth, dark green elliptical leaves with uniform cellular integrity
Healthy terminal growth and abundant blossom set
No leaf spot, mosaic mottling, or edge necrosis
actions: Maintain consistent drip watering to prevent blossom end rot
Provide support stakes to hold heavy fruit branches
preventative: Maintain regular scouting for thrips, mites, and aphids

symptoms: Dark brown to black lesions featuring concentric rings ('target-board' pattern)
Lesions surrounded by chlorotic yellow halo on older lower foliage
Premature leaf desiccation and vine collapse under stress
actions: Apply protective fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin) upon first lesion detection
Ensure adequate nitrogen and potassium fertilization to reduce vine vulnerability
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip or furrow irrigation to minimize leaf wetness
preventative: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Rotate fields on a 3-year cycle with corn, small grains, or legumes

symptoms: Water-soaked irregular pale-to-dark green lesions turning rapidly necrotic and black
White delicate fuzzy mildew sporulation on lesion undersides during humid mornings
Rotting tubers showing granular copper-brown dry rot beneath the skin
actions: Apply systemic fungicides (mefenoxam, cymoxanil, fluopicolide, or cyazofamid) immediately
Destroy and bury infected vines prior to harvest to prevent tuber contamination
Alert local agricultural extension services to track regional late blight spore tracking
preventative: Destroy all potato cull piles and volunteer potato sprouts before spring planting
Ensure wide plant spacing and plant resistant cultivars where available

symptoms: Lush, upright composite leaves with vibrant green coloration
No foliar blight spots, viral curling, or beetle defoliation
Sturdy stems supporting normal vegetative growth and stolon tuberization
actions: Maintain hilling around plant bases to shield developing tubers from sunlight
Monitor soil moisture sensors to maintain 65–80% available water capacity
preventative: Scout weekly for Colorado potato beetle larvae and leafhoppers

symptoms: Vibrant serrated leaves with pale green undersides
Clean floricanes and primocanes free of spur blight or anthracnose cankers
Normal blossom and berry cluster development
actions: Prune spent floricanes to the ground immediately following berry harvest
Ensure mulch coverage along row berms to preserve root moisture
preventative: Maintain trellis wires to keep canes elevated above damp soil

symptoms: Trifoliate dark emerald leaves with uniform smooth texture
Vigorous node development and active nodulation on roots
Absence of frogeye leaf spots, rust pustules, or sudden death syndrome chlorosis
actions: Scout fields during R1–R3 reproductive stages for pod-feeding pests
Monitor soil moisture and rainfall accumulation
preventative: Practice annual crop rotation with corn to break nematode and fungal cycles

symptoms: White talcum-powder circular patches appearing on older leaves and petioles
Foliage becomes yellow, brown, and brittle, senescing prematurely
Fruit exposed to direct sun scald with reduced flavor and yield
actions: Apply potassium bicarbonate, sulfur, or quinoxyfen fungicide at earliest symptom onset
Remove heavily infected older runner leaves to increase sunlight inside the vine hill
Irrigate strictly at root level using drip lines or soaker hoses
preventative: Select powdery mildew-resistant squash and pumpkin hybrids
Plant with wide between-row spacing to promote air circulation

symptoms: Numerous small, irregular purple to dark brown spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots coalesce causing leaf margins to curl upward, dry, and appear scorched
Purple lesions on calyxes causing fruit browning and unmarketable berries
actions: Apply protective fungicides (captan or thiophanate-methyl) during early flowering
Renovate strawberry beds after harvest by mowing and burning or removing dead foliage
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation during warm humid evenings
preventative: Plant certified virus and fungal-indexed strawberry runners
Mulch beds with clean wheat straw or black plastic

symptoms: Trifoliate glossy dark green leaves with clean serrated margins
Vigorous crown development with abundant blossom trusses
Absence of leaf spot, scorch, or botrytis gray mold
actions: Maintain consistent drip irrigation during fruit expansion
Ensure proper straw mulch to elevate fruit away from damp soil
preventative: Regular field scouting for two-spotted spider mites and tarnished plant bugs

symptoms: Small, dark brown to black circular lesions with greasy or water-soaked halos
Lesions become angular and translucent with age
Sunken, scabby, rough dark spots on green and ripe tomato fruit
actions: Apply fixed copper sprays tank-mixed with mancozeb to overcome copper tolerance
Disinfect greenhouse stakes, pruning tools, and tomato clips
Avoid overhead irrigation and keep field traffic out while leaves are wet
preventative: Source certified bacterial-tested seeds or perform hot-water seed treatment (50°C for 25 min)
Enforce a 3-year rotation away from solanaceous crops

symptoms: Concentric target-board rings surrounded by yellow chlorotic halos on lower foliage
Progressive lower leaf yellowing, browning, and premature defoliation
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions developing near fruit stem attachments
actions: Prune and safely destroy lower infected foliage (do not compost)
Apply chlorothalonil, copper hydroxide, or difenoconazole spray on dry afternoons
Switch overhead irrigation to root-zone drip irrigation
preventative: Apply 5–8cm organic mulch around plant bases to prevent rain-splash inoculum
Stake plants and maintain 60cm spacing for optimal air ventilation

symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked grayish-green lesions that rapidly turn brown and greasy
Delicate white fungal mycelium visible on leaf undersides in high humidity
Large golden-brown firm rot lesions on green fruit, destroying the crop in days
actions: Apply targeted oomycete fungicides (mandipropamid, cymoxanil, or fluopicolide) immediately
Remove and bag heavily infected plants to stop airborne sporangia dispersion
Keep canopy as dry as possible and eliminate potato cull piles nearby
preventative: Plant resistant tomato cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant, Plum Regal)
Monitor regional late blight forecasting networks

symptoms: Pale green to yellow diffuse spots on upper leaf surfaces
Dense olive-green to gray velvety mold growth on corresponding lower leaf surfaces
Older leaves wither and die while hanging on the vine
actions: Lower greenhouse or polyhouse humidity below 85% by increasing ventilation and heat
Apply copper-based fungicides or biofungicides (Bacillus subtilis)
Prune lower suckers and dense canopy leaves to improve air circulation
preventative: Plant tomato cultivars possessing Cf resistance genes
Space plants generously in protected cultivation structures

symptoms: Numerous small circular spots with dark brown margins and gray or tan centers
Tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) clearly visible in center of spots
Severe defoliation moving progressively from lower canopy upward
actions: Strip and remove infected bottom leaves up to the lowest fruit cluster
Apply chlorothalonil or copper fungicide every 7 to 10 days during rainy weather
Ensure mulch layer covers all exposed soil under the tomato canopy
preventative: Rotate fields out of tomatoes and eggplants for at least 2 years
Cleanly cultivate or remove all tomato residues post-harvest

symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling and speckled flecks across upper leaf surfaces
Delicate, silky webbing on leaf undersides and terminal growing tips
Leaves become bronzed, desiccated, and drop under heavy mite feeding
actions: Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus)
Apply insecticidal soap, neem oil, or selective miticides (bifenazate)
Douse underside of leaves with high-pressure water spray to disrupt webs
preventative: Avoid dusty orchard conditions and maintain balanced, non-excessive nitrogen
Monitor hot, dry microclimates where mite reproductive cycles accelerate

symptoms: Small, pinpoint brown spots that expand into circular lesions with light brown centers
Dark concentric rings resembling a target board with yellow halos
Depressed, pitted lesions with dark margins on mature fruit
actions: Apply strobilurin or carboxamide fungicides according to IPM thresholds
Improve canopy aeration by staking, trellising, and pruning suckers
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation
preventative: Rotate fields with non-host grass or corn crops
Control broadleaf weed hosts (such as sicklepod) around field edges

symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaf margins
Interveinal yellowing (chlorosis) and distinct reduction in leaf size
Stunted, bushy plant stature and complete cessation of fruit flower set
actions: Strictly control the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci) using systemic insecticides or insecticidal soaps
Install 50-mesh insect netting on greenhouse vents and entrances
Rogue out and destroy infected viral plants immediately in sealed bags
preventative: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g., Tygress, Skyway, Charger)
Maintain a 2-month host-free fallow window between cropping cycles

symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaf surfaces
Distorted, filiform ('shoestring') leaf growth and leaf wrinkling
Internal brown necrotic rings inside fruit wall tissue
actions: Wash hands and dip tools in non-fat dry milk solution (20%) or trisodium phosphate
Strictly prohibit tobacco smoking or handling near tomato plants (prevents mechanical transfer)
Immediately remove and burn infected plants to halt field spread
preventative: Plant ToMV-resistant varieties carrying the Tm-2 or Tm-2^2 resistance alleles
Use certified viral-free seed treated with trisodium phosphate

symptoms: Vibrant deep green composite leaves with turgid upright petioles
Clean terminal shoot growth and vigorous blossom clusters
Absence of foliar spotting, yellowing, or insect feeding marks
actions: Maintain consistent root drip irrigation to preserve soil moisture balance
Inspect undersides of leaves weekly for aphids and whiteflies
preventative: Maintain sturdy stakes, prune lower ground suckers, and inspect soil pH
